I think the main problem is, she does not really "teach" anything. I mean, apparently, this is her style. She comes to the class, starts a never-ending brainstorm session, every student participates (yaaay) and talks about their deep knowledge (i.e.: POLS 101 or IR 101) trying to impress her, she listens and writes what they say to the board anyway. And then, you're waiting as a regular student, "Okay, Ms. Ozcurumez, let's put this modern, fancy talk aside, I'm glad that you let me talk, but please start talking about what's wrong, what's right, what's relevant or irrelevant here. When will you clearly indicate, separate, differentiate, compare, contrast, classify and explain things? When will you give me the knowledge that I need to pass this course and actually *learn* about all those states' policies?" Well, this rarely happens. She assumes that you already "read the chapter" and now you know most of the things about it. She is gently tapping the topics that "you're supposed to know" and raises the questions, here comes the brainstorm session again, you're listening incredibly hard, waiting for that eye-opening explanation, but there is none. What you're supposed to know for her course is that "read the chapters" regularly by yourself, and simply take care of your own thing. As said, this is her strategy and she's no nanny for any student. It's *your* responsibility to learn and know. I respect her style, she decides so, I get it, but this strategy was a disappointment for me. I'd prefer, as a regular student -call me lazy, I don't care- a conventional style in which a lecturer literally and precisely *teaches* and keeps the brainstorming short.
